problem: Find the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)=2\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)\,k.$
worked_solution:
To find the domain of $f$, we need the intersection of the domains of the individual components.

- The domain of the 1st component $2$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 2nd component ${t}^{2}$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 3rd component $\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)$ is $t\in (-1,\infty ).$

The intersection is illustrated in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/44e047a975ee3b2ad7966b95bbba3a6270925f451c8cb8c6dac6dbef532f2b7a.png)

Therefore, the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is $t\in (-1,\infty ).$

We write the position of a point (vector) in spherical polar coordinates as $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ),$ where 

- $\rho \ge 0$ is the distance from the point to the origin,

- $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ is the angle between the point and the positive $x$-axis, and

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$ is the angle the corresponding vector makes with the positive $z$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/d338181a6631c513330ef2dd3899cfb9b01cb6f4c4ff7d9cd65038b381e7fec4.png)

  

Notice that inside our region, the spherical polar coordinates vary withing the following domains:

- $\rho \in [0,3]$

- $\theta \in [\frac{3\pi }{2},2\pi ]$

- $ϕ\in [0,\pi ]$

Therefore, we have

$$
{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

A type I region can be written as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le x\le b,\,g(x)\le y\le f(x)},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type I region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $x:$

$$
x=\sqrt{3-y}+1\,⟹\,y=3-(x-1)^{2}
$$

The function $y=0$ is already written as a function of $x.$

Notice that the region lies between the vertical lines $x=1$ and $x=2.$ So, we have $0\le x\le 1.$

We draw a vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower function $g(x)$ and the upper function $f(x).$ A vertical line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type I region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/be799df2140d3a437bb311427dcae0e297cb6bd3844f88932157eb6ace6e7e59.png)

The vertical line enters the region through the lower function $y=0$ and leaves through the upper function $y=3-(x-1)^{2}.$ So, we have $0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3-(x-1)^{2}}.
$$

The center of mass, denoted $\overset{―}{x},$ of a collection of point masses ${m}_{1},{m}_{2},…,{m}_{n}$ located at ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ along the $x$-axis is given by 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m},
$$

 

where 

- $m={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}$ is the total mass of the system,

- ${M}_{O}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i}$ is the total moment of the system about the origin $O.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{1} & =4, & \,{m}_{2} & =6, & \,{m}_{3} & =8, \\ {x}_{1} & =-3, & \,{x}_{2} & =-1, & \,{x}_{3} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total mass of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}+{m}_{2}+{m}_{3} \\  & =4+6+8 \\  & =18\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

and the moment of the system about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & ={m}_{1}{x}_{1}+{m}_{2}{x}_{2}+{m}_{3}{x}_{3} \\  & =4\cdot (-3)+6\cdot (-1)+8\cdot 3 \\  & =-12-6+24 \\  & =6\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\overset{―}{x}=\frac{{M}_{O}}{m}=\frac{6}{18}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The sum and constant multiple rules for double summations state that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{ij}, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}k{a}_{ij} & =k{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying these rules to the given sum, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}2({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}({a}_{ij}+{b}_{ij}) \\  & =2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}{a}_{ij}+2{\sum }_{i=1}^{70}{\sum }_{j=1}^{80}{b}_{ij} \\  & =2\cdot 75+2\cdot 70 \\  & =150+140 \\  & =290.\end{aligned}
$$

The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/fc71859cb4d1e58ea3d15c2da66bce014898281fe237f2e0c2396f96c84c9e79.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093183/assets/eff037b96b6a42120fdfa112a98d1e0749cdd56bd89acd647db448b08d7323ad.png)

So, in this case, the interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<2,\,-1<y<0\,}.
$$
